title: compare() finds bit64::as.integer64(0) and NA_integer64_ equal
description:
```r
waldo::compare(bit64::as.integer64(0L), bit64::NA_integer64_)
# ✔ No differences
```

AFAIU it's because `num_proxy()` never gets invoked because:

```r
identical(bit64::as.integer64(0L), bit64::NA_integer64_)
# [1] TRUE
```

So the `is_identical()` fast path exits immediately:

https://github.com/r-lib/waldo/blob/d9075e4488a45e4189d79f7847b54fcd94a29fff/R/compare.R#L202-L204
https://github.com/r-lib/waldo/blob/d9075e4488a45e4189d79f7847b54fcd94a29fff/R/compare.R#L423-L434

title: Tolerance applies in a surprising way to large integers
description:
``` r
library(waldo)

dt <- as.POSIXct("2016-07-18 16:06:00", tz = "UTC")
compare(dt, dt + 5)
#> `old`: "2016-07-18 16:06:00"
#> `new`: "2016-07-18 16:06:05"
compare(1468857960, 1468857965)
#> `old`: 1468857960
#> `new`: 1468857965

(tol <- testthat::testthat_tolerance())
#> [1] 1.490116e-08
compare(dt, dt + 5, tolerance = tol)
#> ✓ No differences
compare(1468857960, 1468857965, tolerance = tol)
#> ✓ No differences
```

<sup>Created on 2022-03-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Compared with `all.equal()` which has different behaviour for POSIXct:

``` r
library(waldo)

dt <- as.POSIXct("2016-07-18 16:06:00", tz = "UTC")
all.equal(dt, dt + 5)
#> [1] "Mean absolute difference: 5"
all.equal(1468857960, 1468857965)
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2022-03-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I don't think the behaviour is correct in either case: the purpose of tolerance is to ignore minor differences that arise due to floating point error, not to ignore differences in integers that can be exactly represented in floating point.

cc @MichaelChirico

title: document how `waldo::compare` and `all.equal` differ for relative numeric comparison
description:
Perhaps this issue is known or has been reported before - in that case, apologies.

`all.equal` uses its first argument to compute the denominator of the relative difference.  `waldo::compare` uses its second argument, leading to differences in behaviour as here:

```
> x <- c( 0.077172645966023900, -0.000266267947825388, -0.01796820303767930,
+        -0.000266267947825388,  0.026773667457362100,  0.00885332514392564,
+        -0.017968203037679300,  0.008853325143925640,  0.03937164346237700)
> y <- c(0.04, 0, 0, 0, 0.04, 0, 0, 0, 0.04)
> tol <- 0.02
> all.equal(x, y, tolerance = tol)
[1] "Mean relative difference: 0.5326904"
> all.equal(y, x, tolerance = tol)
[1] TRUE
> waldo::compare(x, y, tolerance = tol)
✔ No differences
> waldo::compare(y, x, tolerance = tol)
`old`: 0.040  0.000  0.000  0.000 0.040 0.000  0.000 0.000 0.040
`new`: 0.077 -0.000 -0.018 -0.000 0.027 0.009 -0.018 0.009 0.039
>
```

`help("compare", package="waldo")` and `help("expect_equal", package="testthat")` don't claim that they are drop-in replacements for `all.equal(...)` and `stopifnot(all.equal(...))`, but that seems to be a prevailing belief.  The situation would be improved with clearer documentation about the correspondence of the arguments.

title: Feature request: allow comparison of numerics to ignore the sign of the values
description:
I'm using testthat snapshots in a package that prepares tidy versions of objects returns by functions from the vegan package. Many of these functions perform ordination, computing eigenvectors, the signs of which are not defined and can vary between CPU family or model.

For snapshots of those objects, I'd like the ability to compare such objects while ignoring the signs - the objects are identical to trivial decimal places up to the sign. I understand that if this were supported in `waldo::compare()` via a toggleable argument, `expect_snapshot_value()` would allow for my use case.

Would you consider this as an allowed comparison modifier?

title: allow ignore_attr=NULL to be FALSE
description:
I am having to `ignore_attr="tzone"` on "weird" platforms, so that something like this is natural:

```r
ignore_attr = if (...) "tzone"
# ...
expect_identical(x, y, ignore_attr=ignore_attr)
# ...
expect_identical(x, y, ignore_attr=ignore_attr)
```

I am mildly averse to writing out `else FALSE` which has the visually unpleasant effect of clearly mixing string+logical types for `ignore_attr`.

So hopefully, it's not too controversial to suggest supporting `if (is.null(ignore_attr)) ignore_attr = FALSE`.

title: comparing UUIDs fail when they differ
description:
Comparing UUIDs works when they are the same, but it fails when they differ. I think it would be preferable to have a fallback of some other sort to indicate the indices where the values differ rather than a failure.

``` r
uuid1 <- uuid::UUIDgenerate(output = "uuid")
waldo::compare(uuid1, uuid1)
#> ✔ No differences
waldo::compare(uuid1, uuid::UUIDgenerate(output = "uuid"))
#> Error in Complex.UUID(x): Re is not supported on UUIDs
```

<sup>Created on 2025-10-23 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

title: srcref diff is shown for S7 classes if there are other differences
description:
``` r
# as expected
library(S7)
#> Warning: package 'S7' was built under R version 4.4.1
fun <- function() {}
waldo::compare(fun, structure(fun, srcref = 1))
#> ✔ No differences
waldo::compare(fun, structure(fun, srcref = 1, foo = 2))
#> `attr(old, 'foo')` is absent
#> `attr(new, 'foo')` is a double vector (2)
waldo::compare(S7_object, structure(S7_object, srcref = 1))
#> ✔ No differences
# unexpected, shouldn't show srcref diff
waldo::compare(S7_object, structure(S7_object, srcref = 1, foo = 2))
#> `attr(old, 'foo')` is absent
#> `attr(new, 'foo')` is a double vector (2)
#> 
#> `attr(old, 'srcref')` is absent
#> `attr(new, 'srcref')` is a double vector (1)
```

<sup>Created on 2025-06-03 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

if there is no difference apart from srcref in `compare_structure()` we don't go further than the `is_identical()`  check but if we do we enter the S7 handling part and `attrs()` doesn't dismiss the "srcref" from the inspection.

Happy to do a PR if it helps.

title: Suggested improvement for "looser" storage rules of Date,POSIXct in R>=4.5.0
description:
```r
x = Sys.Date()
y = seq(Sys.Date(), length.out = 1L, by=1L)
waldo::compare(x, y)
# `old` is an S3 object of class <Date>, a double vector
# `new` is an S3 object of class <Date>, an integer vector
waldo::compare(format(x), format(y))
# ✔ No differences
```

I think this makes writing tests a bit too fussy -- mostly we don't care about this storage difference. Roughly, only R itself should care if behavior of the class differs depending on the storage mode; some exceptions to that can be tested with e.g. `expect_type()` if needed.

title: Comparing large integer vectors slow
description:
## Problem
Comparing large (>1e6) integer vectors can be prohibitively slow after shuffling one vector.

RE: #116 I tried setting `options(diffobj.max.diffs = 50)`, but this didn't help.

## Reprex

```r
v1 <- rep(1:50L, 1e6L / 50L)
v2 <- rep(1:50L, 1e6L / 50L)

v2 <- v2[sample.int(length(v2)]

bench::system_time(
    waldo::compare(v1, v2)
)
# process    real 
# 4.87m   4.87m 
```

## Use Case
Integer indexes are commonly used in `data.table` for RDBMS style relational modelling. As a result of this slow comparison for integer vectors, comparing such `data.table`s is unreasonably slow (~5 minutes * number of columns).

This prevents adoption of `testthat` >= 3.0 in packages using largeish tables. (EDIT: I guess this isn't technically true, since examples in tests should be small, but it would be nice to be able to compare large tables).

The problem also exists for `base::data.frame` but since joins are so much slower the use case isn't as compelling.

title: [enhancement] return differences in objects as R code that can be used to document & reproduce changes in DF
description:
Thanks for the very useful package!

It would be additionally helpful in there could be an option in waldo that would allow the result of a comparison to be returned in terms of R script code that be used to recreate the actual changes that have been made to a dataframe. That way if needed a R user could make a particular sporadic change to a dataframe, document the result of that change to the dataframe, and then use the returned R script to reproduce the change in the dataframe. 

Please see the example that one developer is currently working on to accomplish this result independent of the Waldo package:

Example of a returned R script result documenting the new dataframe's cell changes after comparing two data frames:

dat[3, 1] <- 0.1
dat[2, 2] <- 5
dat[1, 3] <- FALSE
dat[3, 4] <- "E"
levels(dat[, 5]) <- c(levels(dat[, 5]), "5")
dat[3, 5] <- "5"
levels(dat[, 6]) <- c(levels(dat[, 6]), "E")
dat[1, 6] <- "E"

(Please see the complete package description at:
https://github.com/matt-dray/tide)

Potentially such a feature would be most useful when added to the DataEditR package:
https://dillonhammill.github.io/DataEditR/

(DataEditR currently includes a feature to export an R script to reproduce the entire changed dataframe but often all that would be needed [and which would be more concise] would be to only generate the R script needed to generate the change in the cells of the dataframe as the tide developer noted above is attempting to accomplish)

Thank you for considering this enhancement.

title: Tolerance behaves differently than (naively) expected
description:
When using `compare` on vectors (lists, data.frames, etc), the `tolerance` paremater works differently than a naive user would expect. Rather than comparing each entry's deviation separately, it considers the mean deviation of all deviating entries. 
While this matches the documented behavior, it probably isn't what a user would intuitively expect.

Contrived minimal example:
```
vec1 <- rep(1, 1000)
vec2 <- rep(1.01, 1000)
vec2[1000] <- 10
waldo::compare(vec1, vec2, tolerance = 0.1)
```
results in
`✔ No differences`
while many users would probably expect to see the last line (and only the last line) highlighted as difference.

title: Inconsistent handling of tolerance can lead to cryptic failure
description:
Symptom
======

```R
> expect_equal(0.105487503092834, 0.10548753, tolerance = 1.5e-7)

Error: 0.105487503092834 (`actual`) not equal to 0.10548753 (`expected`).

actual != expected but don't know how to show the difference
```
Encountered while using `testthat` but debugging shows the problem lies in `waldo`, and so filing this report here.

Summary Analysis
============
The outer calls lead to `waldo`'s `num_equal` which applies the tolerance to $|x-y|/|y| < \delta$ as long as $|y|>\delta$ where $\delta$ is the tolerance.  Equivalently, it checks $|x-y|<\delta |y|$. Having discovered the difference, it then turns it over to `compare_numeric()` which, I think, attempts to show only as many digits as are necessary to show the difference.  However, the logic here ignores the fact that the absolute difference that causes the test to fail is usually $\delta |y|$, and just uses $\delta$.

With the values shown above this means it's one digit short of what it needs to show the difference; since the numbers agree before that point there are *no* differences in the formatted values and so the list of (string) differences to be shown is empty.  The result is the that `compare_numeric()` reports the "don't know how to show the difference error."

Possible Fix
=======
In `min_digits()`,
https://github.com/r-lib/waldo/blob/e31e97de04105491dcb03a921911af2f4eb16dd2/R/compare-value.R#L161
use instead
```R
  if (!is.null(tolerance)) {
   if (abs(y)>tolerance)
       tolerance <- tolerance*abs(y)
    n <- min(n, digits(tolerance))
  }
```
Although this *may* solve the immediate problem, it does not address the fact that the logic for interpreting the tolerance is living in at least 2 separate places, which seems undesirable.

Fuller Analysis
=========
Here's the call stack, with the innermost call on the top

> num_equal takes a tolerance arg -> FALSE
> 3.2. compare_numeric produces
>  actual != expected but don't know how to show the difference
> 3.1. num_equal  says they don't match even though difference is -2.7e-8 and tol is 1.5e-7.  x is 0.105, and so it must be doing  relative tolerance.  (it divided average absolute diff among those that differ by average y for same, unless average y < tolerance)
> x = 0.105487503092834
> y = 0.10548753
> 3. compare_vector
> 2. compare_by_attr -> empty string
> 1. compare_terminate-> empty string
> compare_structure
> waldo::compare
> waldo_compare
> expect_waldo_equal
> expect_equal

The numbers indicate calls made in sequence: `compare_structure()` first called `compare_terminate()` which returned an empty string, then `compare_by_attr()` and finally `compare_vector()`.  The latter first called `num_equal()` which said the arguments were not equal, and then `compare_numeric()` which first decided there were differences and then, after processing them, decided there weren't any.

The formatting weirdness between the stack line starting with `2.` and the one with `1.` is not intentional or significant; I just don't know how to prevent it.

Related Issues
=========
As my note on `num_equal()` suggests, I found the interpretation of the tolerance surprising, consistent with #188 (at least with with scalar comparison I wasn't exposed to the average difference approach that it apparently uses).  At least in `waldo` it is documented; in `testthat` the tolerance parameter is named, but absolutely no information on its exact meaning appears.

I think, related to #142, this is quite slow but also the output when it does appear is not very informative. I've just come to recognise these types of results where nothing matches as a likely out-of-order problem, and I just re-run waldo but first sort both data sets into what I assume will be a sensible order.

It would be great if waldo could somehow highlight the sort order differences: e.g. `old sort order is likely x, y, z but the new sort order is likely x, z, y` I guess that's probably a crazy complicated problem to solve though!

An alternative stand-in suggestion would for waldo to first check the head and tail of the dataset (first and last 20 records for instance) and if there's no or almost no agreement there, just give up and report those results, rather than trying to compute and report results for the entire data set.

title: Documentation request: how to compare environments?
description:
As part of testthat 3e migration for lintr (https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/pull/910), I'm trying to replace this `expect_equal()` test comparing two environments whose content is identical:

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/aafba478622c6f43c3fb329c69945c36a4d94b68/tests/testthat/test-cache.R#L164

With <3e, it dispatches to `all.equal()` and voila.

With the stricter tests in `waldo::compare()`, however, it's not so simple.

I was unable in a brief search to determine what one should do to compare environments themselves:

 - there's no `compare_proxy.environment`
 - ?waldo::compare only mentions environments as regards `ignore_formula_env` and `ignore_function_env` (not really relevant here)
 - `expect_equal(e1, e2, ignore_attr=TRUE)` _doesn't_ work, which seems to partially contradict ?waldo::compare ("For backward compatibility with all.equal(), you can also use TRUE..." -- which suggests we will get equivalent behavior to the old `expect_equal()` by setting `ignore_attr=TRUE`)
 - no mention of environments on the landing page: https://waldo.r-lib.org/
 - no vignettes

So I'm left wondering what's the recommended approach here.

The simplest fix is `expect_identical(as.list(e1), as.list(e2))`, but it does feel a bit hacky.

title: Slow comparison of large data frames
description:
Comparing large data frames with `waldo::compare()` is relatively slow and increases dramatically with the number of rows. Memory allocation is also quite heavy as a function of the number of rows.

Here are some quick benchmarks. Comparing two tibbles with 10k rows and completely different values in the `x` column takes ~10s and requres 1.5GB of memory. If there's only one difference (`tbl_10k_1`) the computation time is much more reasonable (2s) but still requires the same about of memory.

``` r
library(waldo)
library(tibble)

x <- xp <- runif(10000)
xp[sample(length(x))[1]] <- runif(1)

bench::mark(
  tbl_100   = compare(tibble(x = runif(100)), tibble(x = runif(100))),
  tbl_10k   = compare(tibble(x = runif(10000)), tibble(x = runif(10000))),
  tbl_10k_1 = compare(tibble(x = x), tibble(x = xp)),
  vec_100   = compare(runif(100), runif(1000)),
  vec_10k   = compare(runif(10000), runif(10000)),
  check = FALSE
)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is disabled.
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 tbl_100     22.75ms  24.83ms   37.3      17.82MB    11.8 
#> 2 tbl_10k      10.83s   10.83s    0.0923    1.51GB     6.09
#> 3 tbl_10k_1     2.33s    2.33s    0.430      1.5GB    18.9 
#> 4 vec_100     23.08ms  23.98ms   40.5      733.3KB     3.85
#> 5 vec_10k       3.95s    3.95s    0.253     9.23MB     0
```

title: Confusing output after replacing values
description:
I noticed this when replacing a subset of the values in one column with values from another. `compare` often represented those differences as an insertion in one spot and a deletion at another, rather than as a simple replacement. This only happened when there were adjacent matching values in the comparison and multiple replacements near each other.

```r
old <- rep("aaaaaaaaaaaa", 10)
new <- replace(old, c(4, 6), "bbbbbbbbbbbb")
waldo::compare(old, new)

#     old            | new               
# [1] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" | "aaaaaaaaaaaa" [1]
# [2] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" | "aaaaaaaaaaaa" [2]
# [3] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" | "aaaaaaaaaaaa" [3]
# [4] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" - "bbbbbbbbbbbb" [4]
# [5] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" -                   
# [6] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" | "aaaaaaaaaaaa" [5]
#                    - "bbbbbbbbbbbb" [6]
# [7] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" | "aaaaaaaaaaaa" [7]
# [8] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" | "aaaaaaaaaaaa" [8]
# [9] "aaaaaaaaaaaa" | "aaaaaaaaaaaa" [9]
```

Instead of indicating that elements 4 and 6 were changed in the above, `compare` suggests that `old[4:5]` were replaced with `new[4]`, and a new element was added between `old[6]` and `old[7]`. It seems to prioritize the fact that `new[5]` matches `old[6]` over the match at element 5 in both. I'm not sure it really matters, but it seemed like an odd way to interpret/describe that difference.

title: diff_element() should probably call enc2utf8() before encodeString()
description:
In R-devel, there have been some recent changes to how encodings are handled. I am not entirely sure what changed, but it cause vctrs to fail on this one build. Notably, this build uses the ISO8859-15 charset rather than UTF-8.

https://www.r-project.org/nosvn/R.check/r-devel-linux-x86_64-debian-clang/vctrs-00check.html

Using the rhub docker image with `rhub::local_check_linux(image = "rhub/debian-clang-devel")`, I was able to reproduce the above two issues, but it looks a little different (The A and degree mark disappear here? I imagine it is still the same issue, just printing differently).

```r
 ERROR
Running the tests in 'tests/testthat.R' failed.
Last 13 lines of output:
  `actual` (vec_unique(x)) not identical to `expected` (`expect`).
  
  `attr(actual[[2]], 'enc2')[[1]]`:   "°C"
  `attr(expected[[2]], 'enc2')[[1]]`: "C" 
  
  `attr(actual[[2]], 'enc3')`:   "°C"
  `attr(expected[[2]], 'enc3')`: "C" 
  Backtrace:
      x
   1. \-vctrs:::expect_identical(vec_unique(x), expect) test-translate.R:126:2
   2.   \-vctrs:::expect_waldo_equal("identical", act, exp, info, ...) helper-vctrs.R:55:2
  
  [ FAIL 2 | WARN 0 | SKIP 35 | PASS 4099 ]
```

I believe that I have tracked this down to a change in `expect_identical()` when waldo is used. When I switch to using the old version of `expect_identical()` that doesn't use waldo, the tests that fail here pass again.

`diff_element()` calls `encodeString()` here:
https://github.com/r-lib/waldo/blob/a083b8380a33f00748f0ac1666158c609f52ab85/R/diff.R#L91

Then in `ses()`, `enc2utf8()` is called:
https://github.com/r-lib/waldo/blob/a083b8380a33f00748f0ac1666158c609f52ab85/R/ses.R#L10-L13

I believe the ordering here is what is breaking this test.

On the above mentioned `"rhub/debian-clang-devel"` docker image, I get the following output. Note that this image is specifically designed to _not_ support UTF-8 (AFAIK).

```r
utf8 <- "\u00B0C"

# No UTF-8 support
utf8
#> [1] "?C"
# But marked as UTF-8
Encoding(utf8)
#> [1] "UTF-8"

# There is latin1 support here
latin1 <- iconv(utf8, from = "UTF-8", to = "latin1")

latin1
#> [1] "°C"
Encoding(latin1)
#> [1] "latin1"

# These strings are considered identical
identical(utf8, latin1)
#> [1] TRUE

# If we wanted to compare these strings with `expect_identical()`:
# Waldo first calls encodeString(), then does enc2utf8()
# Note that encodeString() loses the marked encoding (it becomes native, i think)
utf8_quote <- encodeString(utf8, quote = "\"")
latin1_quote <- encodeString(latin1, quote = "\"")

utf8_quote
#> [1] "\"?C\""
Encoding(utf8_quote)
#> [1] "UTF-8"

latin1_quote
#> [1] "\"°C\""
Encoding(latin1_quote)
#> [1] "unknown"

# now we try and use enc2utf8() on these as waldo does
utf8_enc <- enc2utf8(utf8_quote)
latin1_enc <- enc2utf8(latin1_quote)

utf8_enc
#> [1] "\"?C\""
Encoding(utf8_enc)
#> [1] "UTF-8"

latin1_enc
#> [1] "\"°C\""
Encoding(latin1_enc)
#> [1] "UTF-8"

# so by the time waldo actually compares them, they look different
identical(utf8_enc, latin1_enc)
#> [1] FALSE
```

If the strings are first converted to UTF-8 with `enc2utf8()`, then `encodeString()` is called, they will remain identical.

title: Feature idea: compare whole sets
description:
First of all, I want to say how much I love this package, it makes debugging and data-peeking so much easier, so thanks a lot.

Another need I frequently encounter during those processes is the comparison of 2 unordered sets: I'd like to know which values of A are in B and which values of B are in A. This is particularly useful before joining tables.

I made a little **draft** function for this, it only outputs the ratio of missings and lacks all those fancy waldo features: 
``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
compare_set = function(x, y){
  xiny = (x %in% y) %>% sum(na.rm = T)
  xinypercent = (x %in% y) %>% mean(na.rm = T) %>% scales::percent()
  yinx = (y %in% x) %>% sum(na.rm = T)
  yinxpercent = (y %in% x) %>% mean(na.rm = T) %>% scales::percent()
  rtn = c(
    glue("x in y = {round(xiny, 2)} / {length(x)} ({xinypercent})"),
    glue("y in x = {round(yinx, 2)} / {length(y)} ({yinxpercent})")
  )
  cat(rtn[1], "\n")
  cat(rtn[2])
  invisible(rtn)
}
```

title: New organisation for diffs
description:
No one particularly likes the current form:

```
`names(x)`:  -'x' 'y' 'z' -'a' 'b' +'c'
```

Instead, it would be easier to read if the differences were on top of each other:

```
names(x): "x" "y" "z" "a" "b" 
names(y):     "y" "z"     "b" 
```

Or for longer strings, they could be next to each other:

```
names(x)
[1] "x" | 
[2] "y" | "y"  [1]
[3] "z" | "z"  [2]
[4] "a" |
[5] "b" | "b"  [3]
        | "c"  [4]
```

And for even longer strings, each could form one element:

```
x[1] - "x" 

x[2]   "y"
y[2]   "y" 

x[3]   "z" 
y[2]   "z"

x[4] - "a"

x[5]   "b" 
y[3]   "b"

y[4] + "c"
```
